options: P&L earned from completed round trips (buying at the bid, selling at the ask) across many trades, independent of where the price ultimately ends up
The total gain or loss on inventory still held at the end of the day
The fees an exchange charges for removing liquidity
The difference between the opening and closing price of the instrument
questions.explain: Spread capture is the textbook market-making profit from the bid-ask spread on completed round trips -- the component most directly tied to execution quality, not market direction.

questions.q: Why can inventory mark-to-market P&L be negative even on a day with strong positive spread capture?
options: Inventory P&L is pure market exposure on whatever position is still held -- unrelated to how well the market-making logic itself performed that day
This combination is mathematically impossible and indicates a calculation error
Spread capture and inventory P&L are always equal in magnitude but opposite in sign
Inventory P&L can only be negative if spread capture is also negative
questions.explain: The maker can earn real spread on hundreds of round trips while still holding a position at the close that happens to move against it -- these are genuinely independent sources of P&L.

questions.q: Under the maker-taker fee model, what happens when an order adds liquidity (rests on the book and gets filled) versus removes liquidity (crosses the spread)?
options: Adding liquidity typically earns a rebate (the exchange pays the maker); removing liquidity typically costs a fee (the taker pays the exchange)
Both adding and removing liquidity cost the same flat fee
Adding liquidity always costs more than removing liquidity
Maker-taker fees only apply to options markets, never equities
questions.explain: The maker-taker model is a deliberate exchange design choice to subsidize resting liquidity -- rebating makers and charging takers -- which is a real, non-trivial part of a market maker's economics.

questions.q: In the lesson's worked example, why does a maker that has to actively cross the spread (from a hard inventory limit forcing an unwind) end up paying the taker fee?
options: Crossing the spread means the maker is removing liquidity on that specific trade, which is the taker's role under the maker-taker fee structure, not the maker's usual resting-order role
Taker fees only apply to the first trade of the day
The maker always pays taker fees regardless of how it trades
This scenario never actually triggers a taker fee
questions.explain: Actively crossing the spread to unwind inventory is, by definition, removing liquidity -- putting that specific trade on the taker side of the fee structure, which is one more real cost of letting inventory run too far.

questions.q: Why does the lesson argue that a single aggregate P&L number is not enough to judge how a market-making desk performed?
options: It hides whether the result came from actual skill (spread capture), market exposure the maker happened to be holding (inventory P&L), or structural rebate income (fees) -- each requires a different response
Aggregate P&L numbers are always inaccurate and should never be trusted
Only spread capture matters; inventory P&L and fees are irrelevant to performance
A single P&L number is actually sufficient and decomposition adds no value
questions.explain: The decomposition reveals which lever (fair-value quality, inventory discipline, or toxicity exposure) actually needs attention -- a desk only looking at the aggregate can't distinguish a genuinely good day from a lucky or unlucky one.
